title: Fusilli with Pesto
subtitle: Spiral pasta with a fresh basil and pine nut pesto
excerpt: Pesto made by hand from basil, pine nuts, garlic, parmesan, and olive oil, then tossed with spirals of fusilli. Simple enough that the quality of each ingredient matters.
sourceNotes: Classic Ligurian pesto genovese; traditionally made with a pestle and mortar, also works well made quickly in a food processor.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the pesto in small portions. Thaw at room temperature and toss with freshly cooked pasta.
recipe.batchNotes: The pesto makes more than you need for one meal. Store extra in the fridge under a thin layer of olive oil for up to a week.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Pesto keeps in the fridge for up to a week topped with olive oil to stop it browning.

content.text: Good pesto is about balance: enough basil to stay green, enough garlic to be lively, enough parmesan to make it rich. Do not heat the pesto or it will turn dark and the basil will taste cooked. Toss it with the pasta off the heat, loosened with a little pasta water.
Toast the pine nuts in a dry frying pan over a medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes until pale gold. Tip onto a plate to cool.

In a pestle and mortar, pound the garlic and sea salt to a paste. Add the pine nuts and pound to a rough paste. Add the basil a handful at a time, pounding after each addition. Alternatively, pulse everything except the oil in a food processor until finely chopped.
Stir in the parmesan. Slowly stir in the olive oil until you have a loose, bright green paste. Taste and adjust salt.
Bring a large pan of salted water to the boil. Cook the fusilli according to the packet, then reserve a large mug of pasta water before draining.
Put the pesto in a large bowl. Add 3 tablespoons of the hot pasta water and stir to loosen.
Add the drained fusilli to the bowl and toss well. Add more pasta water as needed until the pesto coats the pasta in a glossy sauce. Serve straight away.

items.symptom: The pesto has turned dark and khaki.
items.cause: The basil was over-processed or the pesto was heated.
items.fix: Pulse briefly in a food processor rather than blending on high; and never put pesto into a hot pan.

items.cause: Too much garlic or the pine nuts were over-toasted.
items.fix: Start with half a clove of garlic and taste before adding more; toast the pine nuts to pale gold only, not brown.

items.symptom: The pesto is too thick to coat the pasta.
items.cause: Not enough pasta water was used to loosen it.
items.fix: Add the hot pasta water a tablespoon at a time to the pesto before the pasta goes in; the starch helps the sauce coat every spiral.
